[EVIDENCE]  
- Progressive, rest-painful left knee swelling for 2 months — classic red flag for low-grade chondrosarcoma (asymptomatic lesions are typical of enchondroma; rest pain suggests active tumor biology).  
- Lytic lesion in distal femur with thin sclerotic rim and “soap bubble” matrix on X-ray — a recognized radiographic pattern of low-grade central chondrosarcoma, reflecting chondroid matrix calcification.  
- Well-circumscribed, non-invasive lesion on MRI — consistent with low-grade (not high-grade) chondrosarcoma, which often lacks aggressive features like cortical destruction or soft-tissue extension.  
- Isolated focal uptake on bone scan — reflects increased metabolic activity of the lesion, aligning with symptomatic, biologically active chondrosarcoma rather than quiescent enchondroma.  
- Pain refractory to ibuprofen — suggests non-inflammatory, neoplastic pain mechanism, not mechanical or reactive.  
- Biopsy explicitly recommended to exclude low-grade chondrosarcoma — indicating clinical suspicion is high and drives diagnostic planning.

[GAPS]  
- Age of patient — critical for differentiating chondroblastoma (<25 yrs) vs. chondrosarcoma (typically >40 yrs); not specified.  
- Histopathology result — definitive diagnosis requires biopsy; currently pending.  
- CT findings — specifically cortical integrity and extent of matrix calcification, which help distinguish enchondroma (mature, ring-and-arc calcifications) from chondrosarcoma (irregular, punctate, or “popcorn” calcifications).  
- MRI signal characteristics (e.g., T2 hyperintensity, presence of fluid-fluid levels, perilesional edema) — edema may support more aggressive behavior.  

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Low-grade central chondrosarcoma
